comment_text.value:
At this point I'd rather try to invest effort and usage in a harness that is FOSS and is actually steered by a non-profit. Goose comes to mind and to be honest I haven't tried it beyond installing and giving it a prompt or two.

Comiong to harnesses, even Pi seems like a weird choice. I mean Pi, until it's "your own customised Pi", is pretty useless and pointless. Besides they are also starting to have their own models/infra business (or is it mostly proxy like OpenCode?).

I have also given up on Herdr and came back to Tmux (and doing a bit of customisation slowly, as I need it). I wanted to try dsh but somehow couldn't brave it. Maybe once I have a good container/vm setup is ready. I know I am biased/discriminatory here, but there are things about which I'd be better safe than sorry.

As for OpenCode: I used V1 a lot and I am struggling with V2 currently. Yes, it just doesn't feel right. It's neither here, nor there. I am not a harness reviewer, so I won't be able to put that into industry accepted words and tests but it doesn't feel useful and right to me. At least Pi is completely stripped (it might be changing though) and then you can make it as you want it. Even Claude Code is better than OpenCode and that's saying something. I find Codex to be quite effective but it doesn't feel familiar. I am still in the middle of some work so I am using OpenCode v2 a lot (and then there's OpenCode Go and I won't want to play around a lot with it) but I will move away. Where? I am not sure yet.

What I feel will work for me? I guess a harness of my own! Forked something smaller/similar? I don't know. No, really! Just like I have never found the "my" notes app and journal app yet, I don't think I should use any of these harnesses if it doesn't work for me, especially now that I can kinda make one (hail LLM/vibe coding :P). It doesn't even have to be a TS/Node monsters most of these harnesses are. More I am reading about, digging deeper (haven't been quite far yet), how models and the "local setup" interact, the more I end up scratching my head – why all this drama and why all these 5 billion GitHub star "harnesses" with trillions of lines of code! Why? It doesn't make sense!

story_title.value: OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why?

comment_text.value:
I am doing tmux + Claude but I wanted a bit more.

Firstly, I want to sandbox my agents from each other and from my hard-drive, and partition (and encrypt) secrets, so I use (and wrote) byre[0], and run a devbox with long-running agents for certain tasks. TermRover[1] is a pretty good SSH client for tmux. For a more native integration I have started using Happier[2] which provides a web front-end and iOS app for my sessions too (unified with real Claude Code, so handover is seamless), and put together a byre skill[3] to make that easy.

[1]: https://termrover.sh/

[2]: https://happier.dev/

comment_text.value:
It is fine to move up a level, and use models with their providers' harnesses, as long as you stay away from extras like their own memory and infrastructure. There is not much investment required, and you will end up with a more robust solution. A simple setup that works:

- Agents live in their own directories, for example ~/Agents/[project]/[instance]/

- In a tmux session run each agent in its own window and directory. Pi, OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex, a combination, whatever works best at any given time.

- Tell them that they are working with other agents, and that knowledge is shared and stored in an agreed format. They are very good at using OKF[1], for example. In my actual setup I use a harvester agent whose only job is to ensure the quality of the knowledge.

- They can communicate with each other simply by sending messages to each other's tmux windows with tmux send-keys. If the team grows, or you work with other people, you can use a general messaging system (I wrote and maintain https://github.com/awebai/aweb but I am sure there are others).

1: https://okf.md

story_title.value: Gemini 4 Argon

comment_text.value:
Hi HN,

I built Ciao to solve problems I was experiencing:

1. Connecting to a new host should be as seamless as possible. I SSH a lot nowadays, and I find the key sharing across devices cumbersome.

2. I get annoyed by setting up insert-your-favorite VPN on new machines. They're all great. I don't want to think about them.

3. There's a lot of harnesses: Claude Code and Codex now have decent mobile push notifications but what about Pi or xyz-shiny-new harness? The harness is another tool that should be abstracted out.

4. I want a single application that has the big picture of all of my agents. Tmux and Herdr are great but they don't have an overview of all my connected machines' agents.

---

With Ciao you curl|sh the daemon --> run ciao pair --> point your phone's camera at the QR code --> and you're connected. It uses iroh for accountless and E2EE connection. There's an optional relay server for APNS which too is E2EE.

One of my favorite aspects of agentic-engineering is being able to just have a lot of fun with programming. Among many features, I built a visually pleasing toggle between terminal-mode and native-chat-mode. If you install Ciao, come back here and tell me what you think.

story_title.value: Ciao, Control coding agents from your phone

comment_text.value:
Nice. That need was one of my initial inspirations for AQ as well. The VPS plus dropped-connections part of your story is very familiar. Two things mattered most when I worked on this same problem:

first, persistence has to live server-side (tmux or equivalent), so the browser tab is only a view and never the owner of the session; if the tab dying can kill work, mobile use stays fragile.

Second, on your security question: the relay path sees every keystroke and whatever secrets scroll through the terminal, so I'd frame it as custody rather than transport. Keep credentials only on the executing machine, make any shareable view a short-lived, token-scoped link with an explicit revoke, and treat Tailscale-first as the default rather than the fallback.

Disclosure: I'm building AQ (aq.dev), which lives in this same problem space (agent sessions that keep running after you close the laptop, joinable from a browser), so I've spent a lot of time on exactly these two questions. We compared the options, including the plain VM plus tmux route, here: https://aq.dev/guides/keep-claude-code-running-after-closing...

story_title.value: Show HN: Tui2web – use any TUI on the web

comment_text.value:
I use something like OpenClaw. For me the big benefit isn't so much the autonomous nature but the organizational structure. The one I use exposes an MCP and lets me control it via talking to an LLM _in the tool_ which is really powerful. EG "audit this", "in X thread we were discussing Y, can you pull that information", etc. And the organizational structure just... makes a ton of sense to me. Don't have to set up a ton of steering and whatnot, it just kinda works.

Being able to use the search to find and resume an old thread is fantastic. The thing I use lets me use whatever underlying CLI that I want, which IMO the biggest limitation on Claude Code or whatnot is that you... have to use Claude models. Sometimes I wanna use sol, sometimes a cheap chinese model, etc. And I want sol with 1m context.

I know there are other tools out there that can do this. I know some people love their tmux/cmux, but IMO the thing that matters the most is being comfy and knowing the tool well. Hell, James Gosling used NetBeans when I talked to him in 2023. Know the tool well and that matters the most, IMO.

For me, it helps with my ADHD brain. And I could spend all day just researching and trying new tools, they are a dime a dozen these days.

Pulling some stats, I have 25 "tabs", and across all of those, I have 1,298 unique threads. 9,539 unique messages.

It works for me, but I don't care about the autonomous part.

story_title.value: OpenClaw 2.0, Accidentally

comment_text.value:
Eh, I don't want the tools I use to stamp their names on everything. It's also not uncommon for me to switch between GPT and Claude or different models in the harness if one of them isn't doing well. GPT-5.6 Terra has been doing a significantly better job at writing concise PR bodies and commit messages than Claude's usual multi paragraph word soup.

I don't need "Created by Claude Code 1.2.3, Opus 4.8 inside tmux inside ghostty on macOS ## on Mac Book Pro 2019 by git 123 in /Users/nijave/repo"

If you want session context, commit the session or prompt or add a git note. I think opaque URIs are the wrong approach unless they're to an issue tracker with more details. Proprietary URIs are not easily usable and interoperable with other tools. Commited information should still be valid and useful in 10 years.

I'm also not sure session is the right level of abstraction. I recently setup Claude Code with subscription delegation to opencode harness with z.ai coding plans and opencode go coding plan and it's been working fairly but there is no singular "session"

story_title.value: Claude Session URL appended to commit messages and PR descriptions by default
